en: The male roles are played by the *sūtradhāra*— the stage director—
and the *pāripāśvika*— the assistant to the stage director.
Three warriors:
Baladeva—the preceptor in mace-fighting to Duryodhana;
Duryodhana—the King of the Kurus.
Aśvatthāman—the son of Preceptor Droṇa;
Durjaya—the son of Duryodhana;
and the women.
Gāndhārī—the mother of Duryodhana;
Pauravī—the queen of the Kuru king;
Mālavī—the queen of the Kuru king.
*Ūrubhaṅga*.
(After the *nāndī*, the Stage Manager enters.
Stage Manager:

Arjuna has crossed that river of enemies— whose banks are Bhīṣma and Droṇa, whose waters are Jayadratha, whose deep pools are the King of Gāndhāra, and which teems with Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, and Kṛpa as its waves, crocodiles, and sharks, while Duryodhana is its current— with the raft of whose arrows and swords for sand he has emerged.
May that Blessed Lord Keśava be your boat for crossing over your enemies. || 1 ||
Thus I address the noble sirs. Ah! While I am thus occupied in addressing you, what is this sound that is heard? Pray, let me see!
(Behind the scenes) Here we are, sir! Here we are!
(Entering) The Assistant: Sir, from where indeed have these [people] come?

Men wander about with their limbs mangled by hundreds of iron arrows and javelins raised for the sake of heaven; their bodies, which served as the touchstone for each other’s prowess, have been scarred by the tusks of rutting lordly elephants. || 2 ||
Sūtradhāra:

My good sir, do you not understand? In the camp of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which is now devoid of the hundred sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and remains only with Duryodhana; in the camp of Yudhiṣṭhira, which remains only with the Pāṇḍavas and Janārdana; and at Samantapañcaka, strewn with the bodies of kings—this is the battle where elephants, horses, lords of men, and warriors have been slain.
Like a painting on a canvas where the lines are blurred and disordered,
when the battle between Vṛkodara and Suyodhana had commenced,
the warriors entered that place which was the sole abode for the destruction of kings.
(They both exit. The prologue ends. (Then enter three soldiers.)
"We are all here, sir! We are here!
First Actor:
It is the abode of enmity, the touchstone of strength, the dwelling-place of pride,
and for men, the assembly hall for the self-choice marriage of Apsarases in battles;
it is the final bed of heroes for kings and the sacrificial rite of offering the breath as an oblation into the fire.
They reached the hermitage known as Raṇasaṃjña, which was accessible to kings by way of the sky.
The second [said]: "You have spoken correctly;
the bodies of the lords of the nāgas are like mountains uneven with rocks."
In every direction, vultures have made their dwellings among the chariots of slain great car-warriors;
these lords of the earth, having attained heaven by performing various deeds while facing the enemy in battle, were long struck down after they themselves had struck others.
The third [verse]: "Thus it is;
the sacrificial post of the trunk of the noble elephant has the arrows fixed as its darbha grass."
With heaps of slain elephants as its high altars, blazing with the fire of heroes,
with banners spread out like canopies, with the loud roar of lions as its sacred mantras, and with fallen animals and men as the sacrificial offerings, the sacrifice of war stood complete.
First:
Your honors, behold this other thing as well:
these [bodies] whose lives have been taken by each other's arrows.
On this ground of the battlefield,
birds with faces like those of flesh-eating demons take up residence; here they make ornaments out of the loosened bodies of kings.
The second [type] is an elephant that has been struck down by the falling of continuous showers of iron arrows, though it was fully prepared and intent on battle.
With his armor shattered, yet still holding his arrow and his bow, he sinks down like a royal armory.
The third:
"Sirs, behold this other thing as well:
[a corpse] with a garland of severed heads made from flower garlands fallen from the tips of banners."
The auspicious wives of his kinsmen joyfully lowered their son-in-law from the front of the chariot— him who, like a warrior fallen from his vehicle, had been the sole arrow of hope for his family.
All:

Oh, how truly terrifying is this Samantapañcaka! Its ground is mired with the blood of slain and fallen elephants, horses, and men; it is strewn with scattered armor, shields, parasols, chowries, tomara-spears, arrows, lances, breastplates, and headless trunks; and it is covered on all sides with weapons such as spears, darts, axes, bhindipāla-javelins, tridents, clubs, mallets, varāhakarṇa-missiles, kaṇaya-shafts, karpaṇa-engines, spikes, swords, and maces.
First:
For here,
indeed, rivers of blood are being crossed, with fallen elephants serving as bridges; horses, driven by charioteers who have collapsed and are deprived of their kings, carry the chariots along.
Headless trunks, with their heads fallen, run about due to former habit; and maddened elephants, devoid of riders, wander here and there. (10)
The second [speaker]:
"Sirs, behold this other thing as well:
these vultures, with tawny eyes raised like *madhūka* buds."
With their sharp beaks acting as goads for the elephants that are the lords of the Daityas,
these birds shine in the sky with their outstretched, long, and scattered wings, appearing like palm-leaf fans fashioned from flesh and coral.
The third [stanza]:
This [army], with its horses, elephants, lords of men, and warriors cast down on all sides by the fierce rays of the sun, has been laid bare.
Strewn with iron arrows, spears, shafts, lances, and swords, the earth seems to bear a fallen host of stars. || 12 ||
The First:

Oh, even in such a state, the Kṣatriyas shine forth with unabated splendor! For here, indeed, their clusters of copper-colored lip-petals are surrounded by swarms of bees in the form of trembling, rolling eyes; and—
With her brow furrowed like a curved filament and her crown-ornaments scattered like withered petals, she—
awakened by the sun of valor at the front of battle and raised upon a bed of iron arrows—
stood motionless like a land-lotus formed by the fearless faces of kings.
The second said: "Since death prevails even over such kṣatriyas as these, it is truly impossible for men in adverse circumstances to maintain their own strength.
The third said:
"Death alone prevails over the Kṣatriyas.
First:
"What doubt can there be?"
The second [said]:
"Do not,

do not touch this bow, which has its string colored by the smoke of the Khāṇḍava forest, which is the destroyer of the Saṃśaptakas, which brought cries of lamentation from heaven, and which was the sacrifice of the life-breaths of the Nivātakavacas."

By means of arrows remaining from his discharge during the battle with Maheśvara, Pārtha, through the power of his weapons, caused kings intoxicated by pride to be received by Death at the front of the fray.
"Everyone—
ah, what sound is this! Are the clouds thundering, or are mountains being pulverized by the falling of thunderbolts?"
Is the earth being torn asunder by thunderclaps terrifying with their tumultuous roar?
Or is it the ocean, having gathered together the caverns and chasms within the belly of Mount Mandara, that is emitting this sound, agitated by garlands of waves restless and shaken by the wind? (15)
Very well, let us observe it for a moment. (All walk about.

First Actor: Ah! This is indeed the mace-duel that has commenced in the presence of Draupadī, who was insulted by the seizing of her hair; in the presence of Bhīmasena, the middle Pāṇḍava, enraged at the slaughter of his hundred brothers; in the presence of Mahārāja Duryodhana, furious over the killing of his kin; and in the presence of the tutelary deities of the Kuru and Yadu clans, headed by Dvaipāyana, Halāyudha, Kṛṣṇa, and Vidura.

The second [verse]: Upon Bhīma’s chest, which was as thick as a beautiful slab of gold, and upon Duryodhana’s shoulder-region, as hard as the trunk of Indra’s elephant— both having been struck and split open.
And from him, as weapons were being struck against the surfaces between their two arms, a sound arose produced by the blows of fierce clubs. || 16 ||
The third:
This is the great king,
whose crown trembles and quivers upon his head, and whose face has eyes like flames of anger.
His body dwarfed by the crushing of his [enemies'] positions, with his forearms raised high,
this mace in his hand— smeared with the mud of his enemies' blood— shines like a great Indra’s thunderbolt accompanied by a meteor, placed upon the summit of Mount Kailāsa.
First:
Let this Pāṇḍava be beheld for now, his limbs drenched with the blood of combat—
his forehead split open and bleeding from the wound, and both his shoulder-joints shattered.
With his chest made wet by the thick blood flowing from his wounds,
Bhima shines with deep gashes moistened by the blood from the blows of the mace; he resembles Mount Meru, its rocks smeared by the drenching of liquid minerals.
The second [hero],
leaping about, hurls his terrible mace, roars,
swiftly seizes his arm, and shatters what has been done by him.
The powerful king, endowed with training and formidable, moves through various maneuvers, advances, and strikes repeatedly. || 19 ||
The third:
This is Vṛkodara,
his body drenched in blood from a deep wound in his head.
Resembling the upholder of the earth and immeasurable in battle,
that king of mountains enters the ground like Mount Hemakūṭa, its minerals loosened and scattered when struck by the thunderbolt.
First:
Having seen Bhīmasena falling, his limbs rendered limp by a severe blow,
Vyāsa stands there in astonishment, holding up his face with a single, focused finger.
Second: "Yudhiṣṭhira falls into despondency here, while Vidura stands with eyes clouded by tears.
Third:
Arjuna has touched the Gāṇḍīva bow, Kṛṣṇa gazes at the sky,
and Rāma, out of affection for his disciple, brandishes his plow as he watches the battle.
The first said: "This is the Great King, an abode of valor, his crown variegated with various jewels, endowed with self-respect, discipline, splendor, and courage."
"O Bhīma! The hero speaks these words in derision: 'Cast away fear; slay the wretched foe in battle! || 22 ||
Second:
Here is Janārdana now, seeing Bhīmasena being mocked, striking his own thigh and imparting some kind of signal.
Third:
Thus consoled by Saṃjñā, the son of the Wind-god gathered his frowns upon the surface of his forehead, wiped away the sweat with his hand,
and, embracing his own mace Citrāṅgadā with both arms, assumed a terrifying countenance.

Beholding his son in distress, he whose eyes are like those of a lion or a bull, having regained strength as if bestowed by the All-pervading One, rises once more from the surface of the earth, roaring.
First:
Ah! The mace-duel has begun once more;
for by him—rubbing his hands upon the ground and vigorously wiping his arms—he [is prepared].
With his lips bitten together, roaring with excessive rage through the power of his prowess,
the son of Gāndhārī— having abandoned righteousness and compassion, and having cast aside the agreement made with Kṛṣṇa— released his mace at the thighs of the son of Pāṇḍu.
All:
Alas! Woe! The great king has fallen! Third:
Seeing the Kuru king falling, his limbs illuminated by the flow of blood, the venerable Dvaipāyana leapt into the sky. He was the one who,

seeing the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) close his eyes out of anger upon witnessing the obstruction of his own vision caused by the plow-wielder’s casual closing of his eyes for the sake of Duryodhana, had himself obstructed Balarāma’s vision with a playful closing of his own eyes.
Perceived by Dvaipāyana through the agitation of his five fingers, Bhīma—his gait supported by the arm of Kṛṣṇa—is led away by the Pāṇḍavas. || 25 ||
First Actor:
Ah! Here too approaches from this very direction the venerable Halāyudha, his eyes wide with impetuosity born of indignation, watching the departure of Bhīmasena.
He is the one whose head is tossed by his movement, and whose long eyes are copper-red with rage.

Having descended to the surface of the earth, he— dragging after him his dark, thin garment that was slipping down— resembled the moon accompanied by its halo, trailing behind it a garland that had been bitten by bees and was being slightly pulled upward.
Second:
Therefore, please come; let us also attend upon the Great King.
Both: [Do so.]
"Very well; this is the primary course of action.
(They exit. Interlude.
Then Baladeva enters.
Baladeva:
O kings! This is not proper.
Having leaped over my plow— the very death of the enemy forces— and disregarding me out of pride because I had set my mind on battle,
he struck that mace upon Duryodhana’s thighs at the head of the fray.
Having been cast down by the excellence of the family discipline, he has fallen. || 27 ||
O Duryodhana! For a moment, let yourself be composed.

[Behold] that which has the remnants of Saubha’s destruction upon its mouth, which is the goad for the crumbling ramparts of the great city of the Asuras, the guide to the waters of the Kālindī, and which is honored by the sacrifice of the life-breaths of enemy forces.
Today, with my plow raised aloft by my hand, I shall turn Bhīma’s broad chest— moist with blood and sweat, thick with mud— into a field of grain strewn with furrows.
(Offstage) May the blessed Halāyudha be gracious, may he be gracious!
Baladeva—

Ah! Even though he has gone this far, the wretched Duryodhana still follows me—this glorious one, whose skin is smeared with blood as red as sandalwood paste from the battle, whose arms are crimsoned by the dust raised as he crawls upon the ground, and who was made to take the vow of a youth. He is like Vāsuki, released by the gods and asuras after the churning for nectar had ended; he was left exhausted in the waters of the ocean while he was still dragging along the serpent’s coils from the mountain.
(Then enters Duryodhana with his two thighs broken.
Duryodhana:
Ah, here I am!
Having violated the established rules of combat by Bhīma,
with his thighs shattered by the blow of the mace,
he was being dragged along the ground by the two arms [of Bhīma].
I carry my own body, half-deceased. || 30 ||
May the Blessed One, Halāyudha, be gracious! May he be gracious!
This head of mine, fallen upon the earth, now prostrates itself at your feet; release your anger today.
Let the funeral offerings for the Kuru lineage, the enmity, the talk of war, and we ourselves be brought to an end.
Baladeva:
O Duryodhana! For a moment, at least, you must sustain yourself.
Duryodhana:
"What will you do?
Baladeva said: "O sir, listen."
With bodies mangled by blows from maces that have torn open their shoulders and hearts, and with plowshares dragged across them,
I shall deliver to you the sons of Pāṇḍu— slain in battle along with their chariots, horses, and elephants— as men who have become your attendants on the journey to heaven.
Duryodhana:
Do not say so!
When Bhīma has fulfilled his vow and departed for heaven, along with the hundred of his brothers—
And when I have departed in this manner, O Rāma, what will the conflict achieve?
Baladeva:
"I am filled with rage because you have deceived me before my very eyes.
Duryodhana: [remains silent]
Baladeva: "You think that I have been deceived;
what doubt is there?"
Duryodhana:
Alas, sir! My life-breaths seem as if they have already been paid for. Why? Because he, with his own intellect, escaped from the house of lac, which was as dreadful as a blazing fire.

O Rāma! If you consider me defeated in this manner by deceit— when in the battle at Vaiśravaṇa’s abode, Bhīma seized the life-breath of the lord of the Hiḍimbās, the Rākṣasa, after his force was repelled by the momentum of an immovable rock— then I have not been conquered.
Baladeva:
Bhīmasena will now remain here, having devised a stratagem for evading battle.
Duryodhana: [What of it?]
"And why was I deceived by Bhīmasena?
Baladeva said:
"Then, by whom were you brought to such a state?"
Duryodhana:
Listen;
by him that *parijātaka* tree of Indra was taken away as if in sport, equal to his own pride, and he who slept for a thousand divine years in the waters of the ocean as if in play.
Having suddenly entered that fierce and terrible mace-duel, which was unpleasant for one who does not seek victory, I have been made to accept death by that Hari, the beloved of the world. (35)
(Offstage) Move aside, move aside, noble sirs! Move aside! (Move aside, move aside, noble sirs!
Baladeva—

(Looking) Ah! Here comes His Majesty Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī, their path guided by Durjaya, accompanied by the women of the inner apartments, their hearts overwhelmed by grief and their gait faltering as they approach from this direction. He is he who— A mine of valor, his eyes distributed among a hundred sons, exultant in pride, with arms reaching down to his golden sacrificial posts—he was surely created by the gods, who were apprehensive regarding the protection of heaven, with his eyes struck by the handfuls of darkness that were his enemies. (36)
(Then enter Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the two queens Gāndhārī and Kuntī, and Durjaya.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
My son, where are you?
Gāndhārī: My dear son! Where are you? The two Queens: [They look around.]
"O Great King! Where are you?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: "Alas! What misery!"
Having heard today in battle that my son has been struck down by deceit,
my face— with tears welling within its eyes— has become utterly blind.
"Gāndhārī! Are you still alive?
Gāndhārī:
"I am still alive, O unfortunate one."
The two queens:
"O Great King! O Great King! The King:

O, what misery! That even my women are weeping! Previously I did not perceive the pain from the blows of weapons, but now I realize it; for my harem women have entered the battlefield with their hair disheveled. || 38 ||
Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
Gāndhārī! Is that man named Duryodhana, who prides himself on his lineage, visible?
Gāndhārī: [He is.]
"O Great King! He is not seen.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"How is it that he is not seen? Alas! Today I am truly blind, I who do not see my son at this time when he ought to be sought. O wretched Kṛtānta!"
Having produced a hundred sons— extremely steadfast heroes who crush their enemies in battle and blaze with human valor—
is that proud man not fit to enjoy the earth scattered across its surface?
Even once, Dhṛtarāṣṭra [received] the funeral offering given by his son. || 39 ||
Gāndhārī:
My son Suyodhana! Give me an answer. Comfort the Great King, who is distressed by the destruction of his hundred sons. Baladeva:

Ah! This is the noble Gāndhārī, whose eyes once felt no curiosity for the faces of her sons and grandsons; she, whose fortitude was swallowed by the grief at Duryodhana’s downfall, now constantly maintains this blindfold over her eyes, made moist by the wounds from weapons.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
My son Duryodhana, O great king of eighteen akṣauhiṇīs! Where are you? King: [He speaks.]
"Today I am the great king.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Come, eldest of my hundred sons; give me an answer!"
The King: Indeed, I shall give an answer; I am ashamed by this report. Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"Come, my son! Pay homage to me.
The King: Here I come! (Gesturing as if rising, he falls. Alas, woe! This is my second blow! Oh, how painful!
Today, by Bhimasena’s striking with his mace and seizing my hair, the salutation to my preceptor’s feet has been stolen from me by my two thighs. (41)
Gāndhārī:
Here you are, my child!
The two queens: [Here you are!]
"Noble lady! We are here. (Ārye! ime svaḥ.
Gāndhārī: "Search for your husband. (Anveṣethāṃ bhartāram.)
The two queens:
Let us go, O unfortunate one! (Let us go, O unfortunate one!
Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"Who is this, sir! Who is pulling at the hem of my garment and pointing out the way?
Durjaya: "Father! It is I, Durjaya. (Father! It is Durjaya.)
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: O grandson Durjaya, seek out your father! Durjaya: [responds]...
"Father! I am indeed exhausted.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"Go, rest upon your father's lap."
Durjaya:
Father! I am going. (Approaching) Father! Where are you? King:
He too has arrived. O, at all times the affection for my son, ever-present in my heart, consumes me. For why?
How indeed will he, who was unacquainted with sorrows and accustomed to sleeping on my lap, speak to me now that he has seen his invincible foe conquered? (42)
Durjaya:
Here is the Great King seated upon the ground. (The King:)
"Son, for what purpose have you come here? Durjaya replied, "Because you were making me wait for so long. (That is, "Because you are taking such a long time.")
The King:
Alas! Even in this state, the affection for a son burns my heart. Durjaya: [He continues:]...
"I too shall indeed sit upon your lap. (He climbs onto his lap.
King—(Stopping him) Durjaya! Durjaya! Oh! Alas!
He who was himself a festival for my eyes and a producer of joy in my heart—this very moon has, through the reversal of time, turned into fire. (43)
Durjaya:
Why do you prevent me from sitting on your lap? (Why do you prevent me from sitting on your lap?
King:
"O son! Having abandoned what is familiar, you must dwell wherever you may be;
from this day forward, this seat formerly occupied by you is no longer yours. (44)
Durjaya:
Where indeed will the Great King go? King:
"I am following my hundred brothers. Durjaya: "Take me there as well. (Lead me also to that place.)
The King: Go, my son! Speak thus to Vṛkodara. Durjaya:
"Come, Great King! You are being sought.
King: My son, by whom?
Durjaya:

"Go, my son! I am not able to come. Durjaya: "I shall take you [with me]. (I will lead you.)
The King:
You are still but a child, my son. Durjaya: [He speaks.]
(Walking around) Noble ladies! Here is the Great King. The two queens: Alas, alas! The Great King! Alas, alas! The Great King!
Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
Where is that great king? Gāndhārī:
"Where is my little son? Durjaya:
"Here is the Great King seated upon the ground."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
Alas, sir! Is this the Great King?
He who is equal in stature to a golden pillar—
It is said that in this world there is but one sovereign lord of the earth;
yet that ascetic has been reduced by me to the ground,
his stature now equal to half the thickness of the door-bolt.
Gāndhārī:
My son Suyodhana! You are exhausted. Rājā: [Sighs]... [He remains silent.]
"I am indeed your son.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: "Who is this, sir?"
Gāndhārī: Great King! I am the mother of fearless sons. King:
"I perceive myself as if born anew today. Oh, father, why this despondency now?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"My son, how shall I not be despondent?"
He whose hundred brothers, arrogant in the strength of their valor and consecrated for the sacrifice of battle, were previously destroyed when you alone were slain. || 46 ||
[He falls. The King:
Alas, woe! His Honor has fallen! Father, comfort her!
Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
My son! Why should I comfort you? Rājā: [He continues: Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Son! Why should I comfort you? Rājā: [He continues:]
"He was slain in battle while facing his foe. O father! Grant me this favor by restraining your grief.
Disregarding even the blazing fire, I have bowed my crest only to your feet;
with that same honor with which I was born, I now depart for heaven.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: For me, an old man who has no desire for life and whose eyes are naturally closed, [this is enough].
Having restrained his fortitude within himself,
the intense grief for his son has begun to overwhelm him.
Baladeva:
O, how tragic!
For Duryodhana, who has lost all hope and whose sight is perpetually extinguished—
I am unable to offer myself to your honor here. || 49 ||
The King: I address her ladyship.
Gāndhārī: [He speaks.]
"Speak, my son! (Speak, my son! The King:
Having paid homage, I say this to you: if any merit has been performed by me...
"In whatever other birth I may take, may you alone be my mother."
Gāndhārī:
You have indeed spoken my own heart's desire.
King: [Listens.]
Mālavī! You too listen:
my brow was knit as if by a falling mace; the space for my necklace was lost by the blood from wounds bursting on my chest, rising at the moment of combat.
Behold these two arms of yours, adorned with golden armlets and scars, possessing full beauty—your husband was not slain while turning his back in battle; why do you weep, O Kṣatriya woman?
Queen: This young woman, my partner in dharma, makes me weep. (This young woman, my partner in dharma, makes me weep.
King:
O Pauravī! You too listen:

through various sacrifices prescribed by the Vedas, you have performed what was desired; your kinsmen have been supported; hundreds of dear ones have been placed above your enemies; and those who sought refuge have not been abandoned.
In battle, eighteen kings with their armies were scorched by my wrath; O proud woman, seeing my indignation at being restrained, women such as you do not weep at all. (52)
Pauravī:
Since I have already resolved to enter [the fire] alone, I do not weep.
King:
"O Darjaya! You too listen.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "O Gāndhārī! What indeed will he say?"
Gāndhārī:
I too think exactly that.
King:
The Pāṇḍavas are to be served by you just as I am; the command of the venerable mother Kuntī is to be carried out. Both Abhimanyu’s mother and Draupadī are to be honored like mothers. Look, my son!
My father Duryodhana was of praiseworthy glory and a heart radiant with self-respect;
he was slain in battle facing his equal. Therefore, abandon your grief in this way.
And having touched Yudhiṣṭhira’s broad arm, which is clad in silk wrapped counter-clockwise,
you must offer water for me along with the sons of Pāṇḍu at the conclusion of the naming ceremony.
Baladeva:
Oh, enmity has turned into remorse! Ah, it is as if there is a sound!
[In this place] silenced by the absence of the roar of the war-drum...
With scattered arrows, armor, fans, and umbrellas,
whose is this roar of the bow that makes the sky filled with flocks of bewildered crows, now that the charioteer and warriors have been slain? (54)
(Offstage) I enter once again that very sacrifice of battle which was commenced by Duryodhana with his bow drawn— now empty, like a horse-sacrifice concluded by the Adhvaryu priest. || 55 ||
Baladeva:
Ah! Here comes the preceptor’s son, Aśvatthāman himself. He is he whose wide eyes are as clear as the petals of a blossoming lotus.
With arms long and reaching down like beautiful golden sacrificial pillars,
he drew this fierce bow with impetuosity,
appearing like Mount Meru with its peaks holding Indra’s rainbow while it is ablaze.
(Then enters Aśvatthāman.

Aśvatthāman—(reciting the same words as previously spoken): O you kings, who once boasted in battle! You whose bodies were mangled by the crocodiles of weapons arising at the moment of the collision of the two armies, oceans of fury in combat; you who remain but a few, with your vital breaths sluggish and bound by gasping sobs! Listen, listen to me!
The lord of the Kauravas has his great arms shattered by my prowess; I am not one whose weapons are slack or fruitless, nor am I the son of a charioteer.
Here, on this ground of victory, I stand today with my weapons raised, ready to be seen.
I alone, the son of Droṇa, stand here impetuously. || 57 ||

What is the use of this glory of victory in battle, which I too have not attained? (Walking about) Wait a moment! While I was intent on pouring the funeral libations for my elders, it is said that the King of the Kurus—the ornament of the Kuru race—was deceived. Who will believe this? For what reason? The eleven kings of the armies, mounted upon chariots and elephants with bows as their only companions, stand with palms joined in reverence, awaiting his command.
Bhīṣma, whose armor was pierced by Rāma’s arrows, and my father Duryodhana, that great chariot-warrior who was clearly victorious in battle—he too has been overcome by Time. (58)

Where indeed has the son of Gāndhārī gone? (Walking about and looking) Ah! Here is the Kuru king, who has crossed the ocean of battle, standing in the midst of a rampart formed by slain elephants, horses, men, and chariots. He, who— With masses of rays from his hair disheveled by the falling of his crown, and with limbs reddened by the blood from wounds caused by the falling of his mace;
he shines like the sun at the end of time, submerged in the twilight, resting upon the rocky surface of the western mountain peak. (59)
(Approaching) O King of the Kurus! What is this? King:
My son’s teacher! It is the fruit of my own dissatisfaction.
Aśvatthāman: O King of the Kurus! I shall win back the very foundation of your hospitality.
The King: [Listens.]
"What will you do? Aśvatthāman replied,
"Listen."

I cast forth Kṛṣṇa, together with the sons of Pāṇḍu, who is prepared for battle, whose body is seated upon the back of Garuḍa, who possesses eight formidable arms and uplifted Śārṅga bow and discus, appearing like a painted canvas covered with a multitude of weapons in the fray. || 60 ||
The King said:
"No, no, do not speak thus!
The entire royal lineage has been consecrated upon the lap of the nurse."
Karna, the son of Śantanu, has gone to heaven with his body fallen;
my hundred brothers have also gone, facing the enemy at the front of battle.
We ourselves have become like this, O son of our preceptor! May you release the bow.
Aśvatthāman: O King of the Kurus!
In battle, when the son of Pāṇḍu seized his mace for the strike, [what happened?]
Today, even your pride has been taken away by your two symmetrical thighs.
The King: Not so! Kings have honor as their very body; it was for the sake of honor alone that I accepted this defeat. Behold, O son of my preceptor!
Draupadī, whose hair was then seized by the hand during the gambling match—
That even a child, Abhimanyu, was slain at the front of the battle;

that the Pāṇḍavas were defeated under the pretext of dice and took refuge in the forest with wild beasts—consider well, O King, what little they have done for me, having been carried away by pride while under the vow of consecration! 63.
Aśvatthāman: In every way, I have made my vow;
I swear it by you, by myself, and by the worlds of heroes.
Having raised a nocturnal battle, I shall consume the Pāṇḍavas in combat.
Baladeva: This which has been uttered by the preceptor’s son will come to pass. Aśvatthāman: [It shall be so.]
Halāyudha: Your Honor is here.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
Alas! This is indeed a deception witnessed by the very eyes.
Aśvatthāman—O Durjaya! Come this way.
To this kingdom, inherited from my father’s prowess and acquired by the strength of my own arms—
"Without formal consecration, become a king by means of the words spoken by the Brahmins. (65)
King:

Ah! My heart’s desire has been fulfilled! My very life-breaths seem to be deserting me. Here are my venerable ancestors, Śantanu and the others; here is the hundredfold host of brothers risen up with Karṇa at their head. And here is Abhimanyu, who, though perched upon the head of Airāvata and grasping the trunk of Indra with his hand, speaks to me in anger. Urvaśī and the other Apsarases have come to me; and here are the great oceans in embodied form.
These are the great rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā. This celestial chariot, capable of carrying heroes, yoked with a thousand swans and sent by Time, has arrived to take me away. Here I come!
(He departs for heaven.
(The curtain falls.)
Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
I am going now to the penance groves, the wealth of the virtuous; for fie upon this kingdom, which has become fruitless through the destruction of my sons!
Aśvatthāman:
Here I come today, with bow in hand, intent upon slaying [the enemy] while they sleep.
(Bharata-vākya)
Baladeva:
May the king, who has subdued the faction of his enemies, protect our earth. (66)
(All exit.
The drama named *Ūrubhaṅga* is finished.
